title: BigQuery basics, joins & CTEs
description: Get comfortable with BigQuery's flavour of SQL, then combine tables with joins, subqueries and common table expressions.

exercises.title: Fully qualified table names
context: In BigQuery every table lives in a **project** and a **dataset**. The full name is written `project.dataset.table`, wrapped in backticks because the project name contains hyphens:
`bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.orders`
In this app you can also write just `orders` — the dataset is set as a default. In the BigQuery console you'll need the full name, so the exercises use it.
instructions: Count the number of orders per `status` in the `orders` table.
Name the count column `num_orders`.
hints: COUNT(*) counts all rows in each group.
The table is called orders, and you group by the column you're counting per.

exercises.title: Dates the BigQuery way
context: Date functions are where BigQuery differs most from PostgreSQL:
- PostgreSQL: `DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at)`
- BigQuery: `DATE_TRUNC(DATE(created_at), MONTH)` — the date part comes **second** and has **no quotes**.
`created_at` is a `TIMESTAMP`, so convert it with `DATE()` first. `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM created_at)` works just like in PostgreSQL. BigQuery also lets you `GROUP BY` and `ORDER BY` a column alias.
instructions: Count the orders per month for orders created in **2023**.
Return the columns `month` (a DATE, the first day of the month) and `num_orders`.
Sort by `month`, oldest first.
hints: The date part is written without quotes: MONTH, YEAR, WEEK …
ORDER BY month sorts ascending by default.

exercises.title: INNER JOIN: revenue per category
context: `order_items` has one row per item sold, and `sale_price` is what the customer paid. The product category isn't stored there — it lives in `products`.
An `INNER JOIN` keeps only rows that have a match in both tables. Link them with `order_items.product_id = products.id`. Table aliases (`AS oi`, `AS p`) keep the query readable.
instructions: Calculate total revenue per product `category`, counting only items with status `'Complete'`.
Return `category` and `revenue`, rounded to 2 decimals.
hints: Revenue is the sum of sale_price.
Join on oi.product_id = p.id. String comparisons are case sensitive: 'Complete'.

exercises.title: LEFT JOIN: customers who never ordered
context: A `LEFT JOIN` keeps **every** row from the left table. When there is no match, the columns from the right table are `NULL`.
That gives a classic pattern — the **anti-join**: left join, then keep only the rows where the right side `IS NULL`. It answers questions like "which customers have never ordered?"
instructions: Count the users in `users` who have **no** rows in `orders`.
Return one column: `users_without_orders`.
hints: Use LEFT JOIN so users without orders are kept.
Unmatched users get NULL in every orders column — filter on o.order_id IS NULL.

requiredPatterns.message: This exercise practises the LEFT JOIN anti-join pattern — use a LEFT JOIN.

exercises.title: Joining three tables
context: Joins chain naturally: each `JOIN … ON …` adds one more table. Products are shipped from a distribution center, so the path is:
`order_items` → `products` (via `product_id`) → `distribution_centers` (via `distribution_center_id`).
`NOT IN ('A', 'B')` excludes several values at once.
instructions: Calculate revenue per distribution center.
Exclude items with status `'Cancelled'` or `'Returned'`.
Return `distribution_center` (the center's name) and `revenue` rounded to 2 decimals.
hints: The third table is distribution_centers, joined on p.distribution_center_id = dc.id.

exercises.title: Subquery in WHERE
context: A subquery is a query inside another query. A subquery that returns a single value can be used anywhere a value is expected — for example in a `WHERE` comparison:
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM …)
instructions: For each `department`, count the products whose `retail_price` is **above the average retail price of all products**.
Return `department` and `num_products`.
hints: The subquery should return one number: AVG(retail_price).
The average is over all products, so the subquery has no GROUP BY.

exercises.title: Your first CTE: average order value
context: A **CTE** (common table expression) is a named subquery defined at the top with `WITH`. It works exactly like in PostgreSQL and makes multi-step logic much easier to read:
WITH step_one AS (
SELECT …
SELECT … FROM step_one
The `orders` table has no order total, so you need to build one from `order_items` first.
instructions: In a CTE called `order_totals`, calculate `order_total` = the sum of `sale_price` per `order_id` and `user_id`, for items with status `'Complete'`.
Join the CTE to `users` and calculate, per `country`: `num_orders` and `avg_order_value` (rounded to 2 decimals).
Only keep countries with **at least 100** orders.
hints: In the main query you select FROM the CTE by its name, just like a table.
Filtering on an aggregate after GROUP BY needs HAVING, not WHERE.

requiredPatterns.message: Solve this one with a CTE: start the query with WITH order_totals AS (…).

exercises.title: Chained CTEs and SAFE_DIVIDE
context: You can define several CTEs in one `WITH`, separated by commas — each can use the ones before it.

The purchase cost of each unit sold is in `inventory_items.cost` (join via `order_items.inventory_item_id = inventory_items.id`). `inventory_items` also has the product's category in `product_category`.
BigQuery has `SAFE_DIVIDE(a, b)`, which returns `NULL` instead of an error when `b` is 0. Use it whenever you calculate ratios.
instructions: CTE `sold`: one row per completed item (`status = 'Complete'`) with `category`, `sale_price` and `cost`.
CTE `category_totals`: per category, `revenue` (sum of sale_price) and `gross_profit` (sum of sale_price − cost).
Final query: `category`, `revenue` and `gross_profit` (both rounded to 2 decimals) and `margin_pct` = gross_profit / revenue × 100, rounded to 1 decimal, using `SAFE_DIVIDE`.
hints: Gross profit per item is sale_price - cost. Margin is SAFE_DIVIDE(gross_profit, revenue).

requiredPatterns.message: Use SAFE_DIVIDE for the margin calculation.

exercises.title: COUNTIF and division without surprises
context: Two BigQuery conveniences:
- `COUNTIF(condition)` counts the rows where the condition is true — a shortcut for `SUM(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.
- The `/` operator **always** returns a FLOAT64. In PostgreSQL `3 / 4` is `0` (integer division); in BigQuery it's `0.75`. No more `* 1.0` tricks!
instructions: Using all rows in `order_items` joined to `products`, calculate per `department`:
`total_items` (all items), `returned_items` (status `'Returned'`) and `return_rate_pct` = returned / total × 100, rounded to 2 decimals.
Use `COUNTIF` for the returned items.
hints: You can't reuse the alias returned_items in the same SELECT — repeat the expressions: COUNTIF(…) / COUNT(*).

requiredPatterns.message: Use COUNTIF to count the returned items.
